title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?
summary: Can misinformation-style interventions help people spot AI-generated media? We ran a registered online survey experiment with U.S. panel respondents (2,257 recruited, 2,030 analysed), randomising them to a control or one of 11 interventions: flagging, provenance labels, automated flagging, an accuracy nudge, breathing and mindfulness exercises, inoculation, and several AI-literacy materials. Respondents then judged posts in a feed. Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 percentage points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and the AI Literacy Guide by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]), while Mindfulness lowered it by 3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]). The pooled accuracy effect was small and inconclusive (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Pooled attitudes toward AI were slightly lower, and some arms

addenda.label: collapse all treated arms vs control in one model

extensions.title: Why does automated flagging help? Sensitivity versus suspicion shift
extensions.hypothesis: Accurate detector labels raise accuracy relative to control and random labels; random labels increase AI-judgments without increasing accuracy.

extensions.title: Does the AI Literacy Guide effect hold for older adults and for audio-visual vs. still-image posts?
extensions.hypothesis: Both the Guide and automated flagging raise accuracy relative to control among adults 55+, with the Guide effect smaller than in the source study.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share of 12 posts correctly classified as AI-generated or real.

extensions.title: Feedback-based practice versus the AI Literacy Guide for spotting AI media
extensions.hypothesis: Practice with feedback raises accuracy more than the passive guide, which in turn does not differ from control.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share of 8 test posts correctly classified as AI-generated or authentic.
